Before the panel, you should know the shape of the group. It is a holding company with three subsidiaries, one of which is a joint venture.
And the reporting line for this role?
Solid line to the Group CFO in Brussels, dotted line to the chief executive here, who runs the Brazilian operation.
Then let me ask the question that matters. When those two disagree, which one actually decides?
That is exactly the right question, and nobody in this process has asked it yet. Brussels decides on capital, and the chief executive decides on people.
Which means a headcount case goes one way and a system case goes the other.
Correct. Now describe the structure you came from, in four sentences, and do not tell me it was difficult.

My line ran to the group chief executive, who sat in London, and I had a dotted line to the finance director, who was the one who decided. It took me six months and one rejected budget to work that out. After that I took the shared service center case to him first, and it was approved in a week.

People assume that when a panel asks about your reporting line they are checking a fact. They are not. The fact is on your CV. What they are testing is whether you understand where power actually sat, and whether you can say it out loud without complaining about it. In a matrix everybody has two bosses and the interesting question is never who signs your objectives. It is who you go to when the two of them disagree. Candidates who describe the chart and stop there sound junior, because a chart is public information. Candidates who describe the chart and then tell you which line was the real one, and how they knew, sound like people who have run something. And by the way, the tone matters more than the content here. The moment a description of a structure turns into a complaint about a structure, we stop hearing an executive and start hearing somebody who did not fit.

What I walked into was a holding company with four subsidiaries, two of which had been acquired eighteen months earlier and had never really been integrated. My formal reporting line was to the group chief executive, who was based in London, and I had a dotted line to the group finance director, who was the person who actually decided things. That distinction cost me about six months to work out. The business units each had their own controller, which sounded sensible on paper and meant in practice that nobody owned a consolidated number. The shared service centre we eventually built was not my idea, and I will say that clearly because people always assume it was. It came from one of the controllers, whose team was doing the same reconciliation four times a month for four different entities.
